title: Factorials and Trailing Zeroes
description: Comprehensive shared preparation notes and worked practice for Factorials and Trailing Zeroes. Review the target examination syllabus and level before reuse.

sections.label: Concepts and worked examples
sections.html:
Factorials and prime exponents

(n!) is the product of the positive integers from 1 through n. To count how many times a prime p divides n!, count multiples of p, then add extra counts for multiples of p^2, p^3, and higher powers: \(\left\lfloor n/p\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor n/p^2\right\rfloor+...\). A multiple of p^2 contributes two factors of p.

Trailing zeroes

Each trailing zero needs one factor of 10, which consists of a factor of 2 and a factor of 5. In a factorial, factors of 2 are more abundant, so count factors of 5 and stop when the quotient is zero.

Worked example: In (\(100!\)), the number of factors of 5 is \(\left\lfloor 100/5\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor 100/25\right\rfloor=20+4=24\), so it ends in 24 zeroes.

Other products and factorial quotients

For a general product, factor each number and pair one 2 with one 5 per trailing zero. For a factorial quotient, subtract prime exponents only after confirming that the quotient is an integer and all terms are defined.

sections.label: Methods and exam checks
sections.html:
• Count multiples of 5 first, then add extra counts for 25, 125 and higher powers.
  • Use repeated division by 5; do not round the quotients.
  • For a general product, the zero count is the smaller of its total number of factors 2 and factors 5.
  • For divisibility, compare prime exponents instead of expanding factorials.
  • Check the scale: n! has fewer than n trailing zeroes for positive n.

sections.label: Key facts and formulas
sections.html:
• Exponent of p in n!: \(\sum_{j\ge1}\left\lfloor n/p^j\right\rfloor\).
  • Trailing zeroes in n!: \(\sum_{j\ge1}\left\lfloor n/5^j\right\rfloor\).
  • For a product with a factors of 2 and b factors of 5, zero count is \(\min(a,b)\).
  • Factorials grow quickly; expansion is unnecessary for these counts.

sections.label: Worked practice
sections.html:
1. Core:

    How many trailing zeroes are in (\(50!\))?

    1. (\(10\))
    2. (\(11\))
    3. (\(12\))
    4. (\(14\))
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(12\))

    Count factors of 5: (\(\lfloor50/5\rfloor=10\)) and (\(\lfloor50/25\rfloor=2\)). Total: 12.

  2. Core:

    How many trailing zeroes are in (\(125!\))?

    1. (\(25\))
    2. (\(28\))
    3. (\(31\))
    4. (\(32\))
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(31\))

    (\(\lfloor125/5\rfloor+\lfloor125/25\rfloor+\lfloor125/125\rfloor=25+5+1=31\)).

  3. Foundation:

    How many trailing zeroes are in (\(200!\))?

    1. (\(40\))
    2. (\(48\))
    3. (\(49\))
    4. (\(50\))
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(49\))

    Count factors of 5: (\(\left\lfloor 200/5\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor 200/25\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor 200/125\right\rfloor=40+8+1=49\)).

  4. Standard:

    What is the greatest exponent e such that (\(5^e\)) divides (\(24!\))?

    1. (\(4\))
    2. (\(5\))
    3. (\(6\))
    4. (\(8\))
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(4\))

    The exponent is (\(\left\lfloor 24/5\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor 24/25\right\rfloor=4+0=4\)).

  5. Challenge:

    How many trailing zeroes are in the product (\(25 \times 16 \times 40\))?

    1. (\(1\))
    2. (\(2\))
    3. (\(3\))
    4. (\(4\))
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(3\))

    There are 7 factors of 2 and 3 factors of 5, so the product has min(\(7,3\))=3 trailing zeroes.
